difficultyReason: The flaw is a subtle scope shift: the economist moves from evidence that a policy 'has not eliminated' an outcome to the conclusion that it 'does not reduce' that outcome. Answer choices use abstract logical vocabulary, and the primary trap (B) describes a genuine necessary/sufficient confusion that sounds like the right kind of structural error but misidentifies what the argument actually does.
stimulus: Economist: Our city's rent-control ordinance has been in effect for fifteen years, yet the percentage of residents living in substandard housing has not declined. Clearly, rent control does nothing to improve housing quality for low-income residents. Other cities that have invested instead in housing voucher programs have seen measurable improvements in housing conditions. We should therefore repeal the ordinance immediately.
questionStem: The economist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that any policy failing to eliminate a problem must have been the cause of that problem

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a condition that is necessary for improving housing quality for one that is sufficient to bring about that improvement

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers that a policy has no beneficial effect solely because it has not produced a complete resolution of the problem it was meant to address

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a causal relationship on the basis of nothing more than a correlation between two variables

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider whether the residents most affected by rent control would support its repeal

explanations.correct: The economist observes that the percentage of residents in substandard housing 'has not declined' — meaning the policy did not eliminate the problem — and leaps to 'does nothing to improve housing quality.' This ignores the possibility that rent control did produce some benefit (e.g., preventing conditions from worsening further, or slowing the rate of deterioration) even though it did not fully resolve the problem. The argument treats absence of complete success as proof of zero effect, which is a scope shift from 'did not eliminate' to 'does not help at all.'
explanations.A: The economist never claims rent control caused substandard housing — only that it failed to reduce it. This trap describes a reversed-causation or post hoc flaw that is not committed here.
explanations.B: The argument makes no move involving necessary or sufficient conditions for improving housing quality. This is a classic necessary/sufficient lure — the right abstract vocabulary for a flaw question, but it misidentifies what the economist actually does. The economist compares two policies, not two logical conditions.
explanations.C: Correct. The economist conflates 'has not produced full resolution' with 'does nothing,' ignoring that the policy might still have reduced the problem relative to what conditions would have been without it.
explanations.D: While the economist does cite other cities' voucher programs favorably, the main conclusion — that rent control 'does nothing' — rests on the failed-to-eliminate inference, not on a correlation between vouchers and improvement. This trap names a real flaw type but mislocates the primary error in the argument.
explanations.E: Resident opinion is irrelevant to whether the policy improves housing quality. This describes an omitted consideration that, while arguably relevant to a policy decision, does not identify the structural reasoning error in the argument.
